notes.text: Ranger 7 is an impact probe from 1964. It is at Sea of Clouds, Moon. Status in the museum: silent.
Before anyone could land on the Moon, people needed to know what the ground looks like up close. That was my job. I launched on July 28, 1964.
I had no legs and no brakes. I was built to fly straight at the Moon and take pictures the whole way down. In my last 17 minutes, my six TV cameras sent back more than 4,000 pictures.

My final pictures showed details only about half a meter across, far smaller than any telescope on Earth could see. Then I crashed into the Moon on purpose, just as planned. The area was renamed Mare Cognitum: the Sea That Has Become Known.
Still out there today: What's left of Ranger 7, scattered around its crash site.
Still out there today: A new name on the map: Mare Cognitum, the Sea That Has Become Known.
Ranger 7's pictures showed that the Moon is covered in craters of every size, even tiny ones. Knowing what the ground looked like up close helped NASA plan how and where to land.
Ranger 8 and Ranger 9 followed in 1965. Then the Surveyor landers touched down gently, and Apollo astronauts came after them.
How did Ranger 7 end its mission? Answer: It crashed into the Moon on purpose while taking pictures. It was built to crash, sending pictures all the way down.
Ranger 7 had six TV cameras. It sent more than 4,000 pictures in its last 17 minutes before impact.
Ranger 7 crashed in a part of the Sea of Clouds that was later named Mare Cognitum, which means 'the Sea That Has Become Known'.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in California built and ran Ranger 7.
Ranger 7 launched on July 28, 1964, and crashed into the Moon on purpose on July 31, 1964.
Its whole trip took about 68 hours. In its last 17 minutes it sent back more than 4,300 close-up photos.
It weighed about 366 kilograms, roughly as much as a grand piano.
Solar panels and batteries powered it.
Ranger 7 rests at: Impact site in Mare Cognitum, between Mare Nubium and Oceanus Procellarum, Moon (10.6340 S, 339.3230 E).
Ranger 7 status (NASA catalog): Destroyed on planned impact; mission complete.
Ranger 7 launched on 1964-07-28, arrived on 1964-07-31 and last contact with Earth was on 1964-07-31.
Ranger 7's mass (NASA catalog): 365.7 kg.
Ranger 7's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 1964-041A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1964-041A.

Orbit view of Ranger 7: Follow the arrow to the small fresh crater Ranger 7 made when it crashed into the Moon in 1964. Photo by Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LROC) (2010), credit NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University.
Surveyor 3 is a robot lander from 1967. It is at Ocean of Storms, Moon. Status in the museum: silent.
Hi! I'm Surveyor 3. In 1967, nobody knew if the Moon's ground was solid or a deep pool of dust that would swallow a spaceship. My job was to find out before any astronaut tried.
I landed in a place called the Ocean of Storms. (It has no water. Early astronomers thought the dark patches were seas!) I used my little robot scoop to dig trenches and poke the soil.
Good news: the ground was firm enough to land on! Two and a half years later, I got visitors. The Apollo 12 astronauts landed close by, walked over, and took my camera home to study.
Still out there today: The Surveyor 3 lander (minus the parts the astronauts took home).
Still out there today: The trenches dug by its scoop.
The Moon's surface could hold up a spacecraft, which helped make the Apollo landings possible.
Surveyor 3 and its robot sisters showed the Moon's ground was safe to land on, so astronauts could follow. About two years later, they did!
What was Surveyor 3 checking before astronauts landed? Answer: If the ground was firm enough to land on. Its scoop showed the soil was solid enough for a lander.
The Apollo 12 astronauts landed near Surveyor 3 in 1969 and brought its camera back to Earth so scientists could see how 2.5 years on the Moon changed it.
Scientists found Earth germs inside the camera after it came home. Many scientists now think the germs got in after it returned to Earth, not that they survived on the Moon.
Surveyor 3 had a robot arm with a scoop. It dug little trenches to test how hard the Moon's soil was.
Hughes Aircraft Company built Surveyor 3, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) managed the mission.
Surveyor 3 launched on April 17, 1967, and landed on the Moon on April 20, 1967.
It worked for about two weeks on the Moon, until the long lunar night.
It weighed about 300 kilograms after landing.
A solar panel and batteries powered it.
It was the first Surveyor to carry a little scoop on a robot arm, so it could dig trenches in the Moon's soil.
Surveyor 3 rests at: Inside a 200 m crater in southeastern Oceanus Procellarum, Moon (3.0162 S, 336.582 E).
Surveyor 3 status (NASA catalog): Inactive since May 1967; Apollo 12 crew removed about 10 kg of parts, including the TV camera, in November 1969.
Surveyor 3 launched on 1967-04-17, arrived on 1967-04-20 and last contact with Earth was on 1967-05-04.
Surveyor 3's mass (NASA catalog): 296 kg (landed); 1,026 kg at launch.
Surveyor 3's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 1967-035A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1967-035A.

Orbit view of Surveyor 3: Find Surveyor 3 inside Surveyor crater, with Apollo 12's Intrepid lander parked on the rim above it. Photo by Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LROC) (2009), credit NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University.
Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage is a lander base (descent stage) from 1969. It is at Sea of Tranquility, Moon. Status in the museum: silent.
I'm the bottom half of the lunar module Eagle. On July 20, 1969, I carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin down to the Moon while Michael Collins circled above in Columbia.
When it was time to go home, the top half of Eagle blasted off and used me as a launch pad. That's why I'm still here, with a plaque on my leg that says the explorers came in peace for all mankind.
My crew left science behind too: a seismometer to feel moonquakes, and a mirror panel called a retroreflector. Scientists on Earth still bounce lasers off that mirror today!
Still out there today: The Eagle descent stage and its plaque.
Still out there today: A U.S. flag.
Still out there today: The laser retroreflector (still used today).
Still out there today: A seismometer for moonquakes (no longer working).
Still out there today: Bootprints!.
Laser beams bounced off the mirror show the Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, about 3.8 cm (1.5 inches) every year.
Five more Apollo crews landed after Eagle. The last, Apollo 17, left the Moon in December 1972. Now NASA's Artemis program plans to send astronauts back.
Why is the Eagle descent stage still on the Moon? Answer: It was used as a launch pad for the top half. The top half (the ascent stage) launched off of it to go home.

The retroreflector is a panel of special mirrors. Scientists fire lasers at it and time how long the light takes to come back. That's how we know the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther from Earth each year.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon. Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module Columbia.
The plaque says that men from the planet Earth first set foot on the Moon in July 1969, and that they came in peace for all mankind.
Astronaut Buzz Aldrin reported the Apollo 11 flag was knocked over by engine exhaust when the top half of Eagle launched.
Grumman Aircraft Engineering built the lunar module, Eagle, for NASA.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969. Eagle landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent about 21 and a half hours on the Moon. The descent stage stayed behind as a launch pad.
The whole lunar module was about 7 meters tall, as tall as a two-story house.
Fully fueled, the lunar module weighed about 15,000 kilograms.
Batteries powered Eagle.
Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage rests at: Tranquility Base, Mare Tranquillitatis, Moon (0.67416 N, 23.47314 E).

Lunar Roving Vehicle is a moon buggy (rover) from 1971. It is at Apollo 15, 16 & 17 landing sites. Status in the museum: parked.
Vroom! I'm a Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Moon buggy. I rode to the Moon folded up against the side of the lunar module, and astronauts unfolded me like a pop-up book.
I run on batteries and drive about as fast as a kid on a bike. With me, astronauts could explore miles away from their lander instead of just walking around it.

There are three of us parked on the Moon: from Apollo 15, 16, and 17. On those trips, astronauts found the 'Genesis Rock', about 4 billion years old, and orange soil made of tiny glass beads from ancient volcanoes.
Still out there today: Three Lunar Roving Vehicles (Apollo 15, 16, and 17).
Still out there today: Tire tracks across the lunar surface.
Driving farther meant finding very old rocks, which helped scientists figure out how the Moon formed.
New Moon rovers are being designed for the Artemis astronauts who will return to the Moon.
How many Moon buggies are parked on the Moon? Answer: Three. Apollo 15, 16, and 17 each left one behind.
The Moon buggy could drive up to about 16 km/h (10 mph), roughly as fast as riding a bike.
The Genesis Rock was found on Apollo 15. It's about 4 billion years old and is a piece of the Moon's ancient crust.
On Apollo 17, astronauts found orange soil. It turned out to be tiny glass beads sprayed out by volcanoes billions of years ago.
The rover ran on batteries, with no gas needed.
Boeing built the Lunar Roving Vehicle for NASA, with the company Delco as a major partner.
Rovers rode to the Moon on Apollo 15 (1971), Apollo 16 (1972), and Apollo 17 (1972).
Each rover was driven for about three days of moonwalks.
It was about 3 meters long and folded up flat to fit on the side of the lunar module.
It weighed about 210 kilograms on Earth, but only about 35 kilograms worth of weight on the Moon.
Two batteries powered it, with an electric motor in each wheel.
Its top speed was about 16 kilometers per hour (10 mph), about as fast as a bicycle.
Lunar Roving Vehicle rests at: Near the Apollo 15 (26.13 N, 3.63 E), Apollo 16 (8.97 S, 15.50 E), and Apollo 17 (20.19 N, 30.77 E) lunar module sites.

notes.text: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package) is a science station from 1969. It is at Five Apollo landing sites on the Moon. Status in the museum: silent.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: Hello from the Ocean of Storms! I'm ALSEP, short for Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package. Astronaut Alan Bean unpacked me on November 19, 1969, during Apollo 12. My central station was switched on that same day, and the astronauts pointed my little antenna at Earth.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: I'm a whole team of instruments spread out on the ground. My seismometer felt the Moon shake, my magnetometer measured its magnetic field, and other sensors studied the solar wind, the thin lunar air, and dust. My power came from a nuclear generator full of plutonium-238. No sunlight needed, so I kept working through the long, freezing lunar nights!
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: Apollo 14, 15, 16, and 17 left ALSEP stations too, so there were five of us radioing science home. When Apollo 12's empty lunar module was crashed into the Moon on purpose, my seismometer recorded the first moonquake ever made by people. On September 30, 1977, NASA turned all of us off. We're still standing right where the astronauts left us.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: Still out there today: Five ALSEP central stations at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17 landing sites.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: Still out there today: Their seismometers, magnetometers, and other instruments, still connected by cables.

notes.text: For up to almost eight years, ALSEP stations measured moonquakes, the Moon's magnetic field, the solar wind, and the Moon's thin atmosphere, giving scientists a look inside the Moon.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: ALSEP showed that science stations can keep working on the Moon long after astronauts leave. NASA is planning new seismometers and science packages for future Moon missions.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: Why could ALSEP keep working through the long, dark lunar night? Answer: A nuclear generator powered it, so it didn't need sunlight. Its plutonium-238 generator made electricity day and night.
notes.source_title: NASA: ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

notes.text: ALSEP seismometers felt the Moon shake. After Apollo 12, the empty top half of the lunar module was crashed into the Moon on purpose, about 60 km away, and the seismometer recorded the first moonquake made by people.

notes.text: Viking 1 Lander is a science lander from 1976. It is at Chryse Planitia, Mars. Status in the museum: silent.
Greetings from 1976! I'm Viking 1, the first NASA spacecraft to land safely on Mars and get to work. I landed seven years to the day after Apollo 11 touched down on the Moon.
I sent home the first pictures taken from the surface of Mars. People were amazed: rusty red rocks, and a sky that wasn't blue.
I had a mini science lab inside me to test the soil for signs of life. My results puzzled scientists for years! I kept working and sending weather reports until 1982.
Still out there today: The Viking 1 lander, silent since 1982.
The first close-up look at Mars' surface and weather, plus experiments that shaped how we still search for life today.
Viking's search for life raised questions that Mars missions are still working on, like the Perseverance rover, which is collecting rock samples today.
What 'first' did Viking 1 achieve? Answer: First picture from the surface of Mars. Viking 1 sent the first photos from Mars' surface.
Viking ran experiments on Martian soil to look for life. The results were confusing, and most scientists concluded they did not show life. The question of life on Mars is still being studied!
Viking 1 was planned for 90 days but kept working for more than six years, until 1982.
Mars' sky looks butterscotch or pinkish in the daytime because of fine dust in the air.
Martin Marietta built the Viking 1 lander. NASA's Langley Research Center led the mission and JPL built the orbiter.
Viking 1 launched on August 20, 1975, and landed on Mars on July 20, 1976.
It worked for more than six years, until November 1982.
The lander weighed about 600 kilograms.
Two small nuclear power generators (RTGs) powered it, so it could work through the Martian winter.
It was the first spacecraft to land safely on Mars and do a full mission there.
Viking 1 Lander rests at: Western Chryse Planitia, Mars (22.27 N, 312.05 E planetocentric); named Thomas Mutch Memorial Station.
Viking 1 Lander status (NASA catalog): Silent since November 1982 (science.nasa.gov gives Nov. 11, after a faulty command).
Viking 1 Lander launched on 1975-08-20, arrived on 1976-07-20 and last contact with Earth was on 1982-11-13.
Viking 1 Lander's mass (NASA catalog): 572 kg (about 600 kg after landing).

notes.text: Sojourner is a rover from 1997. It is at Ares Vallis, Mars. Status in the museum: silent.

I'm Sojourner, the very first rover to drive on Mars! I'm only about the size of a microwave oven. I landed on July 4, 1997, riding inside the Mars Pathfinder lander, which bounced down wrapped in giant airbags.
I drove super slowly and carefully, sniffing rocks with a special instrument to find out what they were made of. Scientists gave the rocks fun names like Barnacle Bill and Yogi.
I was only supposed to work for a week, but I kept going for almost three months! I talked to Earth through my lander, so when the lander went quiet, so did I.
Still out there today: The Sojourner rover.
Still out there today: The Pathfinder lander, renamed the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
Proved small rovers could explore Mars, paving the way for every bigger rover since.
Sojourner proved rovers could work on Mars. In 2004, two much bigger rovers followed: Spirit and Opportunity.
How big is Sojourner? Answer: About the size of a microwave oven. Small but mighty.
Pathfinder landed by bouncing across Mars wrapped in big airbags, then rolled to a stop and opened up like a flower.
Sojourner was named after Sojourner Truth, who fought for freedom and equal rights in the 1800s.
The science team nicknamed rocks so they could talk about them easily. Barnacle Bill and Yogi were two rocks Sojourner studied.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built Sojourner.
Sojourner launched on December 4, 1996, and landed on Mars on July 4, 1997, with the Mars Pathfinder lander.
It was planned to work for 7 days, and it kept going for about 83 days.
It was about 65 centimeters long, about the size of a microwave oven.
It weighed about 10.6 kilograms.
A small solar panel on its back powered it.
Its top speed was about 1 centimeter per second.
Sojourner rests at: Ares Vallis, Mars (19.33 N, 33.55 W), near the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
Sojourner status (NASA catalog): Silent since Sept. 27, 1997, when contact with the lander was lost.
Sojourner launched on 1996-12-04, arrived on 1997-07-04 and last contact with Earth was on 1997-09-27.
Sojourner's mass (NASA catalog): 463 kg (Mars Pathfinder lander, NSSDCA); rover 10.6 kg (NASA mission page).
Sojourner's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 1996-068A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1996-068A.

Orbit view of Sojourner: "MPF" marks the Mars Pathfinder lander, Sojourner's home base. Its parachute lies to the south. Photo by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE) (2006-12-21), credit NASA/JPL/Univ. of Arizona/USGS.
Opportunity is a rover from 2004. It is at Meridiani Planum, Mars. Status in the museum: silent.
Hi, I'm Opportunity, 'Oppy' to my friends. My twin, Spirit, landed on the other side of Mars a few weeks before me in 2004. We were each planned to work for 90 Martian days.
I found tiny round pebbles that scientists called 'blueberries'. They formed in water! That was strong proof that long ago, Mars had water on its surface.
I kept exploring for almost 15 years and drove more than a marathon. In 2018 a giant dust storm covered the sky, my solar panels couldn't get sunlight, and I went quiet.
Still out there today: Opportunity, silent since a 2018 dust storm.
Clear evidence that liquid water once existed on Mars' surface.
Bigger rovers followed in Oppy's tracks: Curiosity landed in 2012 and Perseverance in 2021.
What did Opportunity's 'blueberries' prove? Answer: Mars once had water. Those little balls formed in water long ago.

You might have heard Oppy's last words were 'My battery is low and it's getting dark.' That's actually a reporter's poetic way of describing its last data. The real message was numbers showing low power and a dark, dusty sky.
Opportunity drove about 45 km (28 miles), more than a full marathon, on another planet!
Spirit was Opportunity's twin. It got stuck in soft sand in 2009 and went silent in 2010.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built Opportunity.
Opportunity launched on July 7, 2003, and landed on Mars on January 25, 2004.
It was planned to work for 90 Martian days, and it lasted almost 15 years, until a huge dust storm in 2018.
It was about the size of a golf cart, with its cameras about 1.5 meters off the ground.
It weighed about 185 kilograms.
Solar panels powered it. Wind sometimes blew the dust off them, which helped it last so long.
It drove about 45 kilometers in total, a marathon on Mars.
Opportunity rests at: Perseverance Valley, western rim of Endeavour crater, Meridiani Planum, Mars (landed at 1.946 S, 354.473 E).
Opportunity status (NASA catalog): Silent since a 2018 dust storm; mission declared complete Feb. 13, 2019 after 45.16 km of driving.
Opportunity launched on 2003-07-08, arrived on 2004-01-25 and last contact with Earth was on 2018-06-10.
Opportunity's mass (NASA catalog): 185 kg.
Opportunity's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 2003-032A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2003-032A.

Orbit view of Opportunity: Follow the arrow to Opportunity, driving across Botany Bay on the rim of Endeavour crater. Photo by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE) (2013-07-08), credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/Univ. of Arizona.
Ingenuity is a helicopter from 2021. It is at Jezero Crater, Mars. Status in the museum: parked.
Bzzzz! I'm Ingenuity, a tiny helicopter that weighs about as much as a bag of flour. I rode to Mars tucked under the Perseverance rover.
Flying on Mars is really hard because the air is super thin, about 1% as thick as Earth's. My blades had to spin around 2,400 times a minute to lift me up.
On April 19, 2021, I made the first powered flight on another planet! I was planned for 5 flights, but I flew 72. In 2024 my blades were damaged, so now I'm parked for good.
Still out there today: Ingenuity, parked in Jezero Crater after its final flight.
Proved that aircraft can fly on other planets, so future missions can explore from the sky.
Ingenuity proved flying on Mars works. Engineers are now studying ideas for bigger Mars helicopters that could carry science tools.
How many flights did Ingenuity make? Answer: 72. It was planned for 5 and made 72.
Ingenuity carried a tiny piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 airplane, the first airplane on Earth.
Mars' air is very thin, so Ingenuity had super-light blades that spun very fast, around 2,400 times a minute.
Ingenuity rode to Mars attached to the belly of the Perseverance rover, which is still exploring.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built Ingenuity, with help from the company AeroVironment.
Ingenuity launched with the Perseverance rover on July 30, 2020, and landed on Mars on February 18, 2021.
It was planned for 5 test flights and flew 72 times, until a damaged rotor blade ended its flights in January 2024.
Its rotor blades were about 1.2 meters from tip to tip.
It weighed about 1.8 kilograms, about as much as a bag of flour.
A small solar panel charged its batteries.
It made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet, on April 19, 2021.
Ingenuity rests at: Jezero Crater, Mars, at the site of its 72nd flight.
Ingenuity status (NASA catalog): Rotor blades damaged on its last flight, Jan. 18, 2024; mission ended Jan. 25, 2024.
Ingenuity launched on 2020-07-30 and arrived on 2021-02-18.
Ingenuity's mass (NASA catalog): About 1.8 kg (helicopter; NSSDCA lists it under Mars 2020, whose rover is 1,050 kg).
Ingenuity's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 2020-052A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2020-052A.

Orbit view of Ingenuity: Look inside the red circle: Ingenuity is so small it shows up as a single dot among the sand ripples. Photo by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE) (2022-02-26), credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona.

Sound from Ingenuity: Ingenuity flying on Mars. The Perseverance rover's microphone recorded Ingenuity's fourth flight from 80 meters (262 feet) away on April 30, 2021. Listen for a low hum under the Martian wind: that is the helicopter's spinning blades, made louder by scientists so you can hear it.
Spirit is a rover from 2004. It is at Gusev Crater, Mars. Status in the museum: silent.
I'm Spirit, Opportunity's twin. I bounced down onto Mars inside giant airbags on January 4, 2004. Three weeks later, my twin landed on the other side of the planet.
My mission was planned to last 90 Martian days. I kept going for more than six years, even after one of my front wheels stopped turning in 2006. I just drove backwards and dragged it along.

That dragging wheel scraped up bright white soil that turned out to be almost pure silica. On Earth, soil like that forms around hot springs and steam vents. In 2009 I got stuck in soft sand, and my last message came in March 2010.
Still out there today: Spirit, stuck for good at a spot called Troy.
Still out there today: Its landing platform, at a site named Columbia Memorial Station.
Still out there today: Its parachute and back shell.
The silica Spirit dug up, along with rocks it studied later, showed that Gusev Crater once had hot water. Places with hot water and rock are the kind of places where tiny life could have lived.
Spirit and Opportunity proved that rovers could last for years. NASA's next rovers, Curiosity and Perseverance, are much bigger and carry whole science labs.
What did Spirit's broken, dragging wheel do? Answer: It scraped up soil that showed Mars once had hot water. Its bad wheel became a digging tool and uncovered the silica.
Spirit and Opportunity were twin rovers with the same design. They landed three weeks apart on opposite sides of Mars in January 2004.
In 2009 Spirit's wheels sank into soft sand at a place called Troy. The team tried for months to free it, then used it as a parked science station until it went silent in 2010.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built Spirit.
Spirit launched on June 10, 2003, and landed on Mars on January 4, 2004.
It was planned to work for 90 Martian days and lasted more than six years, until 2010.
It was about the size of a golf cart, with its cameras about 1.5 meters off the ground.
It weighed about 185 kilograms.
Solar panels powered it.
It drove about 7.7 kilometers in total.
Spirit rests at: Troy, beside Home Plate, Gusev Crater, Mars (landed at 14.572 S, 175.478 E).
Spirit status (NASA catalog): Stuck in soft sand since 2009; silent since March 2010; mission ended May 25, 2011 after 7.73 km of driving.
Spirit launched on 2003-06-10, arrived on 2004-01-04 and last contact with Earth was on 2010-03-22.
Spirit's mass (NASA catalog): 185 kg.
Spirit's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 2003-027A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2003-027A.

Orbit view of Spirit: The bright dot just left of the pale plateau Home Plate is Spirit, stuck in soft soil at "Troy." Photo by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE) (2009-06-13), credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona.
Phoenix Mars Lander is a polar lander from 2008. It is at Near the north pole of Mars. Status in the museum: silent.
I landed near the north pole of Mars on May 25, 2008. The ground there is cracked into polygon shapes, like a giant honeycomb, because of the ice underneath.
I dug little trenches with my robotic arm and found bright white chunks. A few days later, some of the chunks had vanished into the thin air. That proved they were water ice!

I also watched snow falling from Martian clouds, though it disappeared before it reached the ground. Then winter came. In the cold and dark my solar panels couldn't make enough power, and my last signal came in November 2008.
Still out there today: The Phoenix lander, with a solar panel probably broken by the weight of winter ice.
Still out there today: The trenches it dug, with names like Dodo-Goldilocks.
Phoenix proved that water ice hides just under the dirt of Mars' arctic plains. It also found a salt called perchlorate in the soil, which could be a useful resource for future human explorers.
Phoenix showed where ice hides on Mars. Future human explorers might one day use ice like that for drinking water and to make rocket fuel.
How did Phoenix know the white chunks were water ice? Answer: They slowly vanished into the air over a few days. In Mars' thin air, the ice turned straight into vapor and disappeared.
Phoenix scraped away dirt and found white chunks just under the surface. Some vanished within a few days, which is what water ice does in Mars' thin, dry air.
Phoenix's laser instrument spotted snow falling from clouds above it. The snow turned to vapor before it reached the ground.
Lockheed Martin built Phoenix. The University of Arizona led the science team, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) managed the mission.
Phoenix launched on August 4, 2007, and landed near Mars's north pole on May 25, 2008.
It worked for about five months, until the Martian winter cut its power in November 2008.
It weighed about 350 kilograms.
Two round solar panels powered it.
Phoenix Mars Lander rests at: Vastitas Borealis, Mars arctic plains (68.22 N, 234.25 E per NASA; nominally 68.15 N, 125.9 W per NSSDCA).

notes.text: InSight Lander is a science lander from 2018. It is at Elysium Planitia, Mars. Status in the museum: silent.
Most Mars explorers study rocks. I wanted to listen to the inside of the planet. I landed on November 26, 2018, on a flat, smooth plain picked to keep me safe.
My robotic arm set a super-sensitive seismometer on the ground. It felt more than 1,300 marsquakes, and even the shaking from space rocks crashing into Mars.

My heat probe, nicknamed 'the mole', was supposed to dig 5 meters down, but the soil was too clumpy and it got stuck near the surface. Over four years, dust piled up on my solar panels until I ran out of power. My last message reached Earth in December 2022.
Still out there today: The InSight lander and its two round solar panels.
Still out there today: Its seismometer, still under its dome-shaped shield.
Still out there today: The heat probe, poking just under the dirt.
By timing how marsquake waves traveled through the planet, scientists measured Mars' insides: its crust, its mantle, and a big core of liquid metal.
Scientists are still studying InSight's quake recordings to learn how rocky planets like Earth and Mars formed.
What was InSight listening for? Answer: Marsquakes. Its seismometer felt more than 1,300 marsquakes.
The heat probe was supposed to hammer itself 5 meters into the ground to measure heat flowing out of Mars. The soil was too clumpy, so it could only get just below the surface.
InSight's seismometer was so sensitive it could feel tiny vibrations. It recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes.
Lockheed Martin built InSight, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) managed the mission. France built its seismometer and Germany built its heat probe.
InSight launched on May 5, 2018, and landed on Mars on November 26, 2018.
It listened for marsquakes for four years, until dust covered its solar panels in December 2022.
It weighed about 360 kilograms.
Two round solar panels powered it.
InSight Lander rests at: Western Elysium Planitia, Mars (about 4.5 N, 135.9 E).
InSight Lander status (NASA catalog): Mission declared over Dec. 21, 2022 after dust cut its solar power; 1,319 marsquakes recorded.
InSight Lander launched on 2018-05-05, arrived on 2018-11-26 and last contact with Earth was on 2022-12-15.
InSight Lander's mass (NASA catalog): 360 kg (landed); about 608 kg at entry.
InSight Lander's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 2018-042A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2018-042A.

notes.text: Sound from InSight Lander: The biggest marsquake ever recorded. On May 4, 2022, InSight's seismometer felt a magnitude 5 quake shake Mars. The shaking was far too low for human ears, so scientists sped up the vibrations to turn them into sound you can hear.

notes.text: Viking 2 Lander is a science lander from 1976. It is at Utopia Planitia, Mars. Status in the museum: silent.

Hi, I'm Viking 2, the twin of Viking 1! I launched on September 9, 1975, and landed on Mars on September 3, 1976. Planners moved my landing spot after photos showed the first choice was too rough, so I settled on a plain called Utopia Planitia.

I landed about 6,460 kilometers from my twin, on the other side of the planet. I sit tilted about 8 degrees, so my pictures make the horizon look crooked! Like my twin, I scooped up soil and tested it for signs of life. My results matched Viking 1's, and scientists still argue about what they mean.

In 1977, during the Martian winter, my cameras spotted thin white frost on the ground around me. Two nuclear generators kept me running for 1,281 Mars days, until my batteries failed in April 1980. Today I'm called the Gerald Soffen Memorial Station, after the Viking project scientist.
Still out there today: The Viking 2 lander, silent since 1980.
Still out there today: Its scoop marks in the soil of Utopia Planitia.
Pictures and weather reports from a second, more northern spot on Mars, including winter frost on the Martian ground.
The two Viking landers set the stage for every Mars lander since, including Phoenix, which found the water ice hidden near the north pole.
What did Viking 2 see on the ground in the Martian winter? Answer: Thin white frost. Its cameras caught frost around the lander in 1977.
Viking 2 landed about 6,460 kilometers (4,000 miles) from its twin, Viking 1, which was at Chryse Planitia.
In 1977 Viking 2 photographed thin white frost near dark rocks around the lander. Scientists thought it was mostly water ice mixed with carbon dioxide.
In 2001 the lander was renamed the Gerald Soffen Memorial Station, after the Viking project scientist.
Viking 2 worked for 1,281 Mars days. It was turned off in April 1980, when its batteries failed.
NASA's Langley Research Center managed the Viking project, working with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL).
Viking 2 launched on September 9, 1975, and its lander touched down on Mars on September 3, 1976.
The lander worked for 1,281 Mars days, until April 1980, when its batteries failed.
The lander weighed about 572 kilograms, not counting fuel.
Two small nuclear generators (RTGs) powered it, with batteries for extra power when needed.
It landed about 6,460 kilometers from its twin, Viking 1, and photographed frost on the Martian ground.
Viking 2 Lander rests at: Utopia Planitia, Mars, 47.6673 N, 134.2809 E, about 200 km west of crater Mie (Gerald Soffen Memorial Station).
Viking 2 Lander status (NASA catalog): silent.

Viking 2 Lander launched on 1975-09-09, arrived on 1976-09-03 (landing) and last contact with Earth was on 1980-04-11 (NSSDCA: turned off when batteries failed; science.nasa.gov gives 1980-04-12 as mission end).
Viking 2 Lander's mass (NASA catalog): 572 kg lander (NSSDCA Facts in Brief); about 600 kg after landing.

Orbit view of Viking 2 Lander: Follow the yellow line to the tiny dark dot: that is Viking Lander 2 on the plains of Utopia. Photo by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE) (2006), credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona.

notes.text: Pioneer 10 is a deep space probe from 1972. It is at Heading toward the star Aldebaran. Status in the museum: silent.
I'm Pioneer 10, launched in 1972. I was the first spacecraft to fly through the asteroid belt. Scientists worried I'd be smashed by space rocks, but I made it!
In 1973 I became the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter, and I sent back close-up pictures of the giant planet.
I sent my last faint signal in 2003. I carry a metal plaque with a drawing of people and a map showing where Earth is, just in case anyone ever finds me.
Still out there today: Pioneer 10, coasting silently out of the solar system.
Still out there today: The Pioneer plaque, a message for anyone who finds it.
Showed spacecraft could safely cross the asteroid belt and survive Jupiter's powerful radiation.
Pioneer 10 showed the way to the outer planets. Its twin Pioneer 11 followed, and then Voyager 1 and Voyager 2.
What was Pioneer 10 the first to do? Answer: Fly through the asteroid belt and past Jupiter. It led the way to the outer solar system.
The Pioneer plaque shows a drawing of a man and a woman, and a map showing where our Sun is, in case anyone ever finds the spacecraft.
Pioneer 10 is drifting toward the star Aldebaran. It would take about 2 million years to get anywhere near it.
TRW built Pioneer 10, and NASA's Ames Research Center ran the mission.
Pioneer 10 launched on March 2, 1972, and flew past Jupiter on December 4, 1973.
It kept talking to Earth for more than 30 years. Its last faint signal came in January 2003.
It weighed about 258 kilograms.
Small nuclear power generators (RTGs) powered it, because sunlight is too weak that far away.
Pioneer 10 rests at: Coasting out of the solar system toward the star Aldebaran (about 2 million years away).
Pioneer 10 status (NASA catalog): Silent; last signal Jan. 23, 2003, from 12.23 billion km.
Pioneer 10 launched on 1972-03-03, arrived on 1973-12-04 and last contact with Earth was on 2003-01-23.
Pioneer 10's mass (NASA catalog): 258 kg.
Pioneer 10's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 1972-012A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1972-012A.
Voyager 1 is a deep space probe from 1977. It is at Interstellar space. Status in the museum: still talking.
I'm Voyager 1, launched in 1977. I flew past Jupiter and Saturn and sent home amazing pictures of their storms, rings, and moons.
In 1990 I turned around and took a photo of Earth from about 6 billion km away. Earth looked like a tiny blue dot in a sunbeam. People call it the 'Pale Blue Dot'.

In 2012 I became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space, the space between the stars. I'm still talking to Earth, though my messages take about a whole day to arrive! I carry a Golden Record with sounds and music from Earth.
Still out there today: Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object.
Still out there today: The Golden Record: greetings, music, and sounds of Earth.
The first measurements from interstellar space, beyond the bubble of the Sun's solar wind.
Its twin, Voyager 2, reached interstellar space in 2018. The two Voyagers are the only spacecraft still sending messages from interstellar space.
What is the 'Pale Blue Dot'? Answer: A photo of Earth taken from very far away. It's Earth, as a tiny speck in a sunbeam.
The Golden Record has greetings in many languages, music from around the world, and sounds like whale songs and laughter, a message about life on Earth.
Voyager 1 is about 26 billion km (16 billion miles) away, farther than any other spacecraft. In November 2026 it reached one light-day from Earth.
Voyager 1 is still sending data, but its power slowly drops each year, so engineers turn off instruments one at a time to keep it going.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built Voyager 1 and still runs it.
Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977. It flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980.
It has been flying for more than 49 years, and in 2012 it became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space.
It weighed about 720 kilograms at launch.
Nuclear power generators (RTGs) power it. Their power slowly fades, so engineers turn things off to save energy.
It travels about 17 kilometers every second.
Voyager 1 rests at: Interstellar space since Aug. 25, 2012; reaches one light-day (25.902 billion km) from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026.
Voyager 1 status (NASA catalog): Operating; magnetometer and plasma wave instruments still on (April 2026).
Voyager 1 launched on 1977-09-05 and arrived on 1979-03-05.
Voyager 1's mass (NASA catalog): 721.9 kg.
Voyager 1's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 1977-084A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1977-084A.

Sound from Voyager 1: Sounds of interstellar space. Voyager 1's plasma wave instrument felt the thin gas between the stars ring after bursts from the Sun hit it in 2012 and 2013. Those waves were turned into these rising tones, and a higher pitch means denser gas, which told scientists Voyager had left our Sun's bubble.
New Horizons is a flyby probe from 2006. It is at The Kuiper Belt. Status in the museum: still talking.
I'm New Horizons, about the size of a grand piano. I launched in 2006 on a long trip to Pluto, so long that the people who built me grew nine years older before I arrived!
On July 14, 2015, I zoomed past Pluto and took the first close-up pictures. Surprise: Pluto has a giant heart-shaped plain of ice!
On New Year's Day 2019, I flew past Arrokoth, the most distant object any spacecraft had ever explored up close. I'm still flying through the Kuiper Belt today.
Still out there today: New Horizons, still exploring the Kuiper Belt.
Pluto is an active world with giant glaciers of ice, not just a frozen rock.
New Horizons is still flying through the Kuiper Belt, sending back science about the far edge of our solar system.
What shape did New Horizons spot on Pluto? Answer: A heart. Pluto's 'heart' is a huge plain of frozen ice.
Pluto's heart is a huge plain of frozen nitrogen ice. Its biggest part is a glacier called Sputnik Planitia, named after Sputnik 1, Earth's first satellite.
Arrokoth looks a bit like a flattened snowman: two lumps stuck together. It's a leftover building block from when the planets formed.
New Horizons took about 9.5 years to reach Pluto.
The Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory built New Horizons, and the Southwest Research Institute leads its science team.
New Horizons launched on January 19, 2006, and flew past Pluto on July 14, 2015.
It is still flying and working. In 2019 it flew past Arrokoth, the most distant world ever explored up close.
It is about the size of a grand piano.
It weighed about 465 kilograms at launch, including its fuel.
A nuclear power generator (an RTG) powers it.
It left Earth faster than any spacecraft before it, about 16 kilometers every second.
New Horizons rests at: Kuiper Belt; passed 60 AU from the Sun on Oct. 1, 2024.
New Horizons status (NASA catalog): Operating; flew past Pluto in 2015 and Arrokoth on Jan. 1, 2019.
New Horizons launched on 2006-01-19 and arrived on 2015-07-14.
New Horizons's mass (NASA catalog): 465 kg at launch, including 80 kg of propellant (Facts in Brief lists 385 kg).
New Horizons's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 2006-001A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2006-001A.
Pioneer 11 is a deep space probe from 1973. It is at Heading out of the solar system toward Sagittarius. Status in the museum: silent.
I'm Pioneer 11, the twin of Pioneer 10! I launched on April 6, 1973. On December 3, 1974, I zoomed past Jupiter, just 43,000 kilometers above its cloud tops.

Then Jupiter's gravity flung me toward Saturn. On September 1, 1979, I became the first spacecraft ever to fly past Saturn. I found a thin new ring outside the main rings, now called the F ring, and a small moon nobody had seen before.

My nuclear generators slowly faded, and in 1995 my team heard from me for the last time. Like my twin, I carry a metal plaque with a drawing of a man and a woman and a map of where we came from. I'm heading toward the center of our galaxy.
Still out there today: Pioneer 11, coasting silently out of the solar system.
Still out there today: Its plaque, a message for anyone who finds it.
The first close-up look at Saturn and its rings, including the discovery of the F ring, plus a second close pass of Jupiter.
Pioneer 11 scouted the path to Saturn. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 followed it there, and later the Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn for 13 years.
What was Pioneer 11 the first spacecraft to do? Answer: Fly past Saturn. It flew past Saturn in 1979, the first spacecraft to get there.
At Saturn, Pioneer 11 found a narrow ring outside the A ring, now called the F ring, and a moon about 200 km across.
Pioneer 10 and 11 each carry a metal plaque, dreamed up by Carl Sagan, showing a man and a woman and where the spacecraft came from.
Regular contact ended on September 30, 1995, when its power got too low to run its science instruments. Engineers caught a few minutes of data on November 24, 1995, and then it went silent.
Pioneer 11 is heading toward the center of the galaxy, in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. In about four million years it will pass near a star in the constellation Aquila.
TRW built Pioneer 11, and NASA's Ames Research Center ran the mission.
Pioneer 11 launched on April 6, 1973. It flew past Jupiter on December 3, 1974, and Saturn on September 1, 1979.
It sent science for more than 22 years. Regular contact ended on September 30, 1995, and its last data came on November 24, 1995.
It weighed about 259 kilograms.
Two nuclear power generators (RTGs) powered it, because sunlight is too weak far from the Sun.
It was the first spacecraft to fly past Saturn, where it found the F ring.
Pioneer 11 rests at: Leaving the solar system toward the galactic center, in the direction of Sagittarius (44.7 AU from the Sun at end of 1995, moving out about 2.5 AU/year).
Pioneer 11 status (NASA catalog): silent.

Pioneer 11 launched on 1973-04-06, arrived on Jupiter flyby 1974-12-03; Saturn flyby 1979-09-01 and last contact with Earth was on 1995-09-30 end of routine operations; last engineering data 1995-11-24.
Pioneer 11's mass (NASA catalog): 259 kg (NSSDCA); 258.5 kg (science.nasa.gov).
Pioneer 11's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 1973-019A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1973-019A.
Dawn is an asteroid belt orbiter from 2007. It is at Orbiting the dwarf planet Ceres. Status in the museum: silent.

Hi, I'm Dawn! I launched on September 27, 2007, with huge solar wings and three ion engines. My engines push out xenon gas so gently it barely feels like a breath, but if you push for years, you go really fast!

In 2011 I became the first spacecraft to orbit something in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter: the giant asteroid Vesta. In 2012 I left Vesta and flew to Ceres, a dwarf planet. In 2015 I became the first spacecraft to visit a dwarf planet, and the first to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth.

On October 31, 2018, I missed my call with Earth. I had run out of hydrazine, the fuel that kept me pointed the right way. I'm still circling Ceres, silent, and my orbit should last at least 20 years, probably more than 50.
Still out there today: The Dawn spacecraft, silently orbiting Ceres.
Vesta and Ceres turned out to be very different worlds, and Dawn's data showed that dwarf planets like Ceres may once have had oceans, and maybe still do.
Dawn showed what ion engines can do. NASA's Psyche spacecraft is now using similar electric thrusters to reach a metal-rich asteroid.
What made Dawn a record breaker? Answer: It was the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth. It orbited Vesta, then Ceres.
Dawn had three ion engines that used electricity from its solar panels to push out xenon gas. The push was tiny, but it could keep going for a very long time.
Dawn ran out of hydrazine, the fuel for the small thrusters that kept it pointed at Earth and the Sun. It missed its scheduled calls on October 31 and November 1, 2018.
Dawn is still orbiting Ceres. Engineers expect its orbit to last at least 20 years, and they are more than 99 percent sure it will last at least 50 years.
Dawn traveled about 6.9 billion kilometers (4.3 billion miles) during its mission.
Orbital Sciences Corporation built Dawn, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) managed the mission.
Dawn launched on September 27, 2007. It orbited Vesta from July 2011 to September 2012 and arrived at Ceres on March 6, 2015.
It worked for 11 years, until it ran out of hydrazine fuel and went silent on October 31, 2018.
It weighed about 1,218 kilograms at launch, including its fuel.
Two large solar arrays made up to about 10 kilowatts near Earth to run its ion engines.
Its ion engines sped it up very slowly but steadily. Over its whole mission it traveled about 6.9 billion kilometers.
It was the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth, and the first to visit a dwarf planet.
Dawn rests at: Uncontrolled orbit around dwarf planet Ceres; expected to last at least 20 years (over 99% confidence of at least 50 years).
Dawn status (NASA catalog): silent.

Dawn launched on 2007-09-27, arrived on Vesta orbit 2011-07-16 (departed 2012-09-05); Ceres orbit 2015-03-06 and last contact with Earth was on 2018-10-31 (missed contacts Oct. 31 and Nov. 1, 2018; out of hydrazine).
Dawn's mass (NASA catalog): 1217.7 kg fueled at launch, 747.1 kg dry (NSSDCA description; its Facts in Brief box says 725 kg).
Dawn's NASA NSSDCA catalog ID is 2007-043A; its catalog page is https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2007-043A.
NEAR Shoemaker is an asteroid orbiter from 1996. It is at The saddle region of asteroid 433 Eros. Status in the museum: silent.

Hi, I'm NEAR Shoemaker! I launched on February 17, 1996. On the way, I flew past an asteroid named Mathilde. Then, on Valentine's Day, February 14, 2000, I became the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid: 433 Eros, a rocky world about 34 kilometers long.
NASA renamed me to honor Gene Shoemaker, a famous geologist who studied craters. I circled Eros for about a year and took around 160,000 pictures.

Then my team tried something wild. I was never built to land, but on February 12, 2001, I touched down gently, at about 6 kilometers per hour. I survived and kept sending science from the surface for about two weeks, until the cold got me. I'm still sitting there on Eros.
Still out there today: NEAR Shoemaker, resting on Eros just south of a saddle-shaped valley called Himeros.
The first close-up, year-long study of an asteroid, mapping Eros from orbit and measuring what it is made of from right on its surface.
NEAR Shoemaker opened the door to asteroid missions like OSIRIS-REx, which brought a sample of asteroid Bennu back to Earth.
What was surprising about NEAR Shoemaker's landing? Answer: It was never built to land, but it survived and kept working. It touched down gently and sent science for about two weeks.
On March 14, 2000, NASA renamed the spacecraft NEAR Shoemaker to honor Eugene Shoemaker, a geologist who helped us understand craters and impacts.
Eros is a peanut-shaped asteroid about 34 kilometers (21 miles) long.
NEAR Shoemaker's last contact was on February 28, 2001. It was too cold, about minus 173 degrees Celsius. NASA tried to call it again in December 2002, but heard nothing.
NEAR returned about 160,000 images, including 69 close-ups taken as it slowly came down to land.
The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory built and ran NEAR Shoemaker for NASA.
NEAR launched on February 17, 1996. It began orbiting Eros on February 14, 2000, and landed on it on February 12, 2001.
It worked for five years. Its last contact was on February 28, 2001, from the surface of Eros.
It weighed about 487 kilograms.
Four gallium arsenide solar panels, each 1.8 by 1.2 meters, powered it.
It was the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid and the first to land on one.
NEAR Shoemaker rests at: Surface of asteroid 433 Eros, in the saddle region just south of Himeros.
NEAR Shoemaker status (NASA catalog): silent.
NEAR Shoemaker launched on 1996-02-17, arrived on Eros orbit 2000-02-14; landed on Eros 2001-02-12 and last contact with Earth was on 2001-02-28 (recontact attempt on 2002-12-10 failed).

notes.text: Kepler Space Telescope is a space telescope from 2009. It is at Drifting in an Earth-trailing orbit around the Sun. Status in the museum: silent.

Hi, I'm Kepler, a planet hunter! I launched in March 2009 and followed Earth around the Sun, trailing a little behind it. I stared at about 150,000 stars at once, watching for tiny dips in their light. A dip means a planet just passed in front of its star.

In 2013 the second of my four reaction wheels broke, and I needed three to point steadily. My engineers had a clever idea: they used the gentle push of sunlight to help balance me, like a kayak in a current. My new mission, called K2, looked at a new patch of sky about every three months.

In October 2018 I ran out of fuel, after more than nine years of work. On November 15, 2018, my team sent my final 'goodnight' commands and turned off my radio. I found more than 2,600 planets, and now I'm drifting quietly around the Sun, far from Earth.
Still out there today: The Kepler Space Telescope, switched off and drifting in its own orbit around the Sun.
Kepler showed that planets are everywhere: our galaxy has more planets than stars, and 20 to 50 percent of the stars in the night sky may have small, possibly rocky planets.
Kepler passed the planet hunt to TESS, a NASA telescope launched in 2018 that searches the brightest, nearest stars.
How did Kepler find planets? Answer: By watching for tiny dips in a star's light when a planet passed in front. A tiny dip in starlight can mean a planet is passing by.
Kepler discovered more than 2,600 planets outside our solar system.
Kepler needed three reaction wheels to point steadily. When a second wheel failed in 2013, engineers used the pressure of sunlight to help balance it. The new mission was called K2.

Kepler ran out of fuel in October 2018. On November 15, 2018, the team sent final commands that turned off its transmitters. That was the same date Johannes Kepler, the astronomer it was named after, died in 1630.
Kepler is drifting in a safe orbit around the Sun, trailing behind Earth. When it was switched off, it was about 151 million kilometers (94 million miles) from Earth.
Ball Aerospace built Kepler, and NASA's Ames Research Center led the mission.
Kepler launched on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral in March 2009.
It collected data for more than nine years. NASA retired it on October 30, 2018, and sent its final commands on November 15, 2018.
It weighed about 1,052 kilograms.
Solar panels powered it.
It found more than 2,600 planets around other stars and watched more than 500,000 stars in all.
Kepler Space Telescope rests at: Drifting in an Earth-trailing orbit around the Sun, about 94 million miles (151 million km) from Earth in Nov. 2018.

notes.text: Apollo 14 golf balls is a hidden treasure from 1971. It is at Fra Mauro, Moon. Status in the museum: parked.
On February 6, 1971, astronaut Alan Shepard had a surprise. He had snuck the head of a golf club onto Apollo 14 and clipped it onto a tool handle meant for scooping up moon dust.
In his stiff spacesuit he could only swing with one hand. He joked that the second ball flew 'miles and miles'. NASA's historians say it really went about 40 yards. Both balls are still up there!
Still out there today: Two golf balls near the Apollo 14 landing site.
Astronaut Alan Shepard brought them, plus a six-iron club head that fit on a tool for scooping up Moon samples.
Apollo 14 launched on January 31, 1971, and Shepard hit the golf balls on February 6, 1971.

notes.text: Charlie Duke's family photo is a hidden treasure from 1972. It is at Descartes Highlands, Moon. Status in the museum: parked.
In April 1972, Apollo 16 astronaut Charlie Duke carried a photo of his family all the way to the Moon.

He left it lying on the ground. Its message says this is the family of Astronaut Duke from Planet Earth, and that it landed on the Moon in April 1972. Nobody knows how it looks after so many years of strong sunlight.
Still out there today: A family photo, lying in the dust at the Apollo 16 site.
Astronaut Charlie Duke left the photo of his family.
Apollo 16 launched on April 16, 1972, and landed on the Moon on April 21, 1972.

notes.text: Apollo 11 goodwill disc is a hidden treasure from 1969. It is at Sea of Tranquility, Moon. Status in the museum: parked.
Apollo 11 left a small silicon disc, about the size of a half-dollar coin, at Tranquility Base. Its shiny surface holds messages from the leaders of 73 countries.
To make them fit, each message was shrunk until it was smaller than the head of a pin. You'd need a microscope to read them!
Still out there today: A silicon disc with goodwill messages from 73 countries.
The disc was made by Sprague Electric, using the same method used to make computer chips, so the messages are tiny.
Apollo 11 astronauts left it on the Moon on July 21, 1969.

notes.text: Moon Wing: Footprints, rovers, and a mirror that still bounces lasers. Everything in this wing is still sitting on the Moon right now.
Moon Wing (Our closest neighbor, 384,000 km away) asks: Can we land on another world, and can people go there?
Mars Wing: No human has ever been to Mars, but our robots have. Some are silent now, but every one of them changed what we know.
Mars Wing (The Red Planet, home of the robot explorers) asks: Was Mars ever a place where life could exist?
Deep Space Wing: Some explorers never landed anywhere. They're still flying, farther from home than anything humans have ever built.
Deep Space Wing (Probes still traveling far beyond the planets) asks: How far can a machine built by people travel?
Hall of Launches: The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts stood about 110 meters tall. That's taller than the Statue of Liberty!
Gallery of Orbits: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. A radio message to Voyager 1 takes about a whole day.
Hall of Footprints: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon, all between 1969 and 1972. With no wind up there, their bootprints could last for millions of years.
Red Dust Corridor: A day on Mars, called a sol, lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes. Mars is about half as wide as Earth.
Signal Room: NASA talks to faraway spacecraft through giant radio dishes in California, Spain, and Australia. Together they're called the Deep Space Network.
Starlight Lounge: The Moon is about 384,000 km away. Driving there at highway speed would take around half a year.
Hall of Rovers: Every NASA Mars rover so far was named by a student who won an essay contest.
Clean Room: Spacecraft are built in super-clean rooms. Engineers wear 'bunny suits' so they don't carry Earth germs to other worlds.

Kuiper Belt (space word): A huge ring of icy worlds beyond Neptune, at the far edge of our solar system. Pluto and Arrokoth live there. Scientists think these icy objects are leftovers from when the planets formed.
Asteroid belt (space word): A wide ring of rocky space rocks between Mars and Jupiter. There are millions of them, but they're so spread out that spacecraft can fly through safely.

Interstellar space (space word): The space between the stars. The Sun blows a bubble of particles around our solar system called the heliosphere. Outside that bubble is interstellar space, where only Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 have been.

Solar wind (space word): A steady stream of tiny charged particles blowing out from the Sun in every direction. It makes the bubble around our solar system and causes the northern and southern lights on Earth.
Lunar module (space word): The two-part spacecraft that carried Apollo astronauts from Moon orbit down to the surface and back up. The bottom half (the descent stage) stayed on the Moon.
Descent stage (space word): The bottom half of the Apollo lunar module. It had the landing engine and legs. When the astronauts left, the top half blasted off and used it as a launch pad.

Retroreflector (space word): A panel of special mirrors that bounces light straight back to where it came from. Scientists fire lasers at the ones on the Moon and time how long the light takes to return, to measure the Moon's distance very precisely.

Seismometer (space word): An instrument that feels the ground shaking. On Earth it measures earthquakes; on the Moon and Mars it measures moonquakes and marsquakes, which tell scientists what the inside of a world is like.
Marsquake (space word): An earthquake on Mars. Mars has no moving plates like Earth, so its quakes come from the planet slowly cooling and shrinking, and from space rocks crashing into it.
Moonquake (space word): An earthquake on the Moon. They're usually small, but some last a long time because the Moon's dry rock rings like a bell.
Crater (space word): A bowl-shaped hole made when a space rock smashes into a planet or moon. Worlds with little or no air, like the Moon, keep their craters for billions of years.

Silica (space word): A mineral made of silicon and oxygen. It's what sand and glass are mostly made of. Nearly pure silica like the soil Spirit found usually forms where hot water and steam flow through rock.

Perchlorate (space word): A salt found in Martian soil. It can be harmful to people, so future astronauts will need to clean it out of anything they use. It also helps water stay liquid at colder temperatures.
Martian day (sol) (space word): A day on Mars is called a sol. It's about 24 hours and 40 minutes long, a little longer than a day on Earth.
Solar panel (space word): A panel that turns sunlight into electricity. Dust and long dark winters are the biggest dangers for solar-powered machines on Mars.

Nuclear power generator (RTG) (space word): A radioisotope thermoelectric generator turns the heat from slowly decaying radioactive material into electricity. It works for decades, with no sunlight needed, which is why spacecraft far from the Sun use them.
Rover (space word): A robot (or a car for astronauts) that drives around on another world to explore it.
Lander (space word): A spacecraft that lands on a planet or moon and stays in one place to do its science.
Orbit (space word): The curved path something takes around a planet, moon, or star, held there by gravity. The Moon orbits Earth, and Earth orbits the Sun.

Radiation (space word): Energy that travels as invisible rays or fast particles. Jupiter is surrounded by very strong radiation that can damage spacecraft electronics, and astronauts need protection from it too.
Plaque (space word): A flat metal sign with writing or drawings on it. The Apollo landers and the Pioneer spacecraft carry plaques as messages for whoever finds them.

Golden Record (space word): A gold-plated copper record on each Voyager spacecraft. It holds greetings in many languages, music from around the world, sounds of Earth, and pictures, as a message about life on Earth.
Pale Blue Dot (space word): A famous 1990 photo taken by Voyager 1 from about 6 billion kilometers away. Earth appears as a tiny speck less than a pixel wide, floating in a beam of sunlight.
Artemis (space word): NASA's program to send astronauts back to the Moon, explore more of it than ever before, and learn how to live and work there before going on to Mars.
Deep Space Network (space word): NASA's giant radio antennas in California, Spain, and Australia. Spread around the globe, they can always talk to faraway spacecraft as Earth turns.
Crust, mantle, and core (space word): The layers inside a rocky planet: a thin rocky crust on top, a thick hot mantle under it, and a metal core in the middle. InSight measured these layers on Mars.
Arrokoth (space word): A small icy world in the Kuiper Belt shaped like a snowman, made of two lumps stuck together. New Horizons flew past it on New Year's Day 2019.
Jezero Crater (space word): A crater on Mars that held a lake billions of years ago. The Perseverance rover and Ingenuity explored it, looking for signs of ancient life.
Ocean of Storms (space word): A huge, dark, flat plain on the Moon made of old lava. Early astronomers thought the dark patches on the Moon were seas, so they named them that way.
Mare Cognitum (space word): Latin for 'the Sea That Has Become Known'. It's the area of the Moon where Ranger 7 crashed, renamed after its pictures.
Polygon ground (space word): Ground cracked into many-sided shapes, like a honeycomb. On Mars and in Earth's Arctic, it forms when ice in the soil freezes and shrinks over and over.
Genesis Rock (space word): A piece of very old Moon rock found by Apollo 15 astronauts. It's more than 4 billion years old and helped scientists learn how the Moon's first crust formed.
Heliosphere (space word): The giant bubble the solar wind blows around our solar system. Its edge is where interstellar space begins.
Inventions and patents: Solving problems in space means inventing things nobody has made before. Many of those inventions end up in everyday life. That's where intellectual property comes in.

notes.text: Inventions and patents, What is intellectual property?: Intellectual property (IP) means creations of the mind: inventions, writing, music, art, names, and logos. IP laws protect these creations so the people who make them get credit and a fair chance to benefit from them.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Four kinds of IP: Patent: protects an invention, like a new machine or process. In the United States a patent usually lasts 20 years from when it's filed. In exchange, the inventor has to publish exactly how the invention works, so everyone can learn from it.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Four kinds of IP: Copyright: protects creative work, like books, music, photos, movies, and computer code. It starts automatically the moment the work is created and saved, written, or recorded.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Four kinds of IP: Trademark: protects names, logos, and slogans that show who makes something. The NASA logo is protected, which is why using it needs NASA's permission.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Four kinds of IP: Trade secret: valuable information a company keeps secret, like a recipe or a way of making something.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Why NASA photos are free to use: Work made by U.S. government employees as part of their jobs is not protected by copyright in the United States. That's why most NASA photos are free to use, and why this museum can show real NASA pictures. We still credit NASA for every one, as NASA asks. A few NASA pictures belong to someone else and say so. The NASA logo is different: it can't be used without NASA's permission.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, NASA's patents: NASA patents many of its inventions. Through its Technology Transfer Program, companies can license those patents (get permission to use them) to build new products. NASA also offers new startup companies licenses with no upfront fee, so new businesses can turn space technology into products.
notes.source_title: NASA JPL: Perseverance pinpoints its location (Ingenuity's phone processor)

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Space inventions you might use: Phone cameras: in the 1990s a team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, led by Eric Fossum, built a tiny, low-power CMOS image sensor to shrink cameras for spacecraft. That kind of sensor is now in phone cameras around the world.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Space inventions you might use: Memory foam: developed in 1966 by engineer Charles Yost for a NASA Ames Research Center project to make airplane seats safer in a crash.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Space inventions you might use: Scratch-resistant lenses: NASA's Ames Research Center made a tough coating to protect plastic surfaces on aerospace equipment, building on its work on astronaut helmet visors. Foster Grant licensed it for sunglass lenses in the 1980s.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Space inventions you might use: Cordless tools: Black & Decker built a battery-powered drill for Apollo astronauts to dig Moon samples. What the company learned helped it improve its cordless tools and create the Dustbuster handheld vacuum.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Space inventions you might use: Tougher tires: Goodyear made a super-strong fiber for the parachute cords that lowered the Viking landers onto Mars. It then used the same material in a radial tire.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Space inventions you might use: A patent you could license: NASA's Glenn Research Center patented an airless "superelastic" tire made of a bendy nickel-titanium metal, designed for future Moon and Mars missions. Companies can apply to license it.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, IP in this museum: Voyager's Golden Record needed permission to include the music on it, because songs are protected by copyright. Carl Sagan wanted the Beatles' "Here Comes the Sun". The Beatles said yes, but their record company, EMI, said no.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, IP in this museum: Ingenuity's brain was a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor, the kind made for smartphones. Ingenuity was the first mission to fly a phone processor in deep space. Sometimes space borrows everyday technology too.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Inventions and patents, Careers: Patent attorneys, patent agents, and IP lawyers help inventors and organizations like NASA protect new ideas. Many of them studied science or engineering first, then law.
notes.source_title: NASA Images and Media Usage Guidelines

notes.text: Space law: Who owns the things left on the Moon? Can a country claim Mars? Space has laws too, and they shape what happens to the machines in this museum.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space law, The Outer Space Treaty (1967): This is the most important space law. More than 100 countries have joined it.
Space law, The Outer Space Treaty (1967): Space is free for every country to explore and use peacefully.
Space law, The Outer Space Treaty (1967): No country can claim the Moon, a planet, or any other place in space as its own territory.
Space law, The Outer Space Treaty (1967): No nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on other worlds.
Space law, The Outer Space Treaty (1967): Countries are responsible for their activities in space, including missions run by private companies.

Space law, The Outer Space Treaty (1967): A country keeps ownership of the objects it launches, even after they land somewhere else. That means the landers and rovers in this museum still belong to the United States.
Space law, Other space agreements: Rescue Agreement (1968): countries promise to help astronauts in trouble and return space objects that land in their territory.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space law, Other space agreements: Liability Convention (1972): if a country's space object crashes and causes damage on Earth or to an airplane, that country must pay for it. For damage in space, it pays if it was at fault.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space law, Other space agreements: Artemis Accords (2020): shared principles for exploring the Moon and beyond peacefully, including protecting historic sites like the Apollo landing areas. The U.S. and seven other countries signed first, and many more have joined since. The Accords are a promise, not a binding treaty.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space law, Protecting the Apollo sites: In 2011 NASA published recommendations asking future Moon missions to keep their distance from the Apollo landing sites, for example by landing at least 2 kilometers away, to protect the bootprints, equipment, and science that are still there. In 2020 the U.S. passed the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act. It requires NASA to make companies and partners it works with on Moon missions agree to follow those recommendations.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space law, Planetary protection: The Outer Space Treaty also says explorers must avoid harmful contamination of other worlds. That's why spacecraft are built in super-clean rooms: so Earth germs don't hitch a ride to Mars and confuse the search for life.
notes.source_title: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance: Planetary Protection

notes.text: Space law, Planetary protection: The Viking landers went even further. Each one was sealed in a protective shell and baked in an oven at about 232°F (111°C) for 40 hours before launch to kill any germs.
notes.source_title: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance: Planetary Protection

notes.text: Space law, Space junk: Old satellites and rocket parts crowd the space around Earth. For years, U.S. guidelines said dead satellites should fall out of orbit within 25 years. In 2022 the U.S. Federal Communications Commission made a new rule: satellites it licenses in low Earth orbit must come down within 5 years after their missions end, so space stays safe for everyone.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space law, Careers: Space lawyers work for space agencies, governments, and companies on contracts, launch licenses, international agreements, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.
notes.source_title: Congress.gov: One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (Public Law 116-275)

notes.text: Space and health: Space is hard on the human body. Keeping astronauts healthy has taught doctors a lot, and some space inventions now help patients on Earth.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space

notes.text: Space and health, What space does to the body: Bones and muscles get weaker without gravity pulling on them, so astronauts on the International Space Station exercise about two hours every day. Exercise slows the loss but doesn't fully stop it.
notes.source_title: NASA: The Human Body in Space

notes.text: Space and health, What space does to the body: Fluids shift toward the head, which can give astronauts puffy faces and can press on the eyes and change their eyesight.
notes.source_title: NASA: The Human Body in Space

notes.text: Space and health, What space does to the body: Radiation is stronger outside Earth's protective magnetic field. Protecting astronauts from it is one of the biggest challenges for a trip to Mars.
notes.source_title: NASA: The Human Body in Space

notes.text: Space and health, The Twins Study: Astronaut Scott Kelly spent 340 days, nearly a year, on the International Space Station while his identical twin, Mark Kelly, stayed on Earth. Comparing the twins helped scientists see how a long spaceflight changes the body. Most changes went back to normal after Scott came home, though a few lasted longer.
notes.source_title: NASA: Landmark Twins Study reveals resilience of human body in space

notes.text: Space and health, Space technology in medicine: Ear thermometers: infrared sensors that JPL developed to measure the temperature of stars and planets were adapted with JPL's help into a thermometer that reads your temperature from your ear in about two seconds.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space

notes.text: Space and health, Space technology in medicine: A heart pump: NASA engineers at Johnson Space Center worked with heart surgeon Dr. Michael DeBakey to design a small pump that helps a weak heart, using what they knew about the Space Shuttle's fuel pumps.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space

notes.text: Space and health, Space technology in medicine: Tiny cameras: the CMOS image sensor invented at JPL for spacecraft is used in medical imaging, including dental X-rays and swallowable camera pills that photograph the inside of the digestive system.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space

notes.text: Space and health, Space technology in medicine: Memory foam has been used in mattresses and pads that protect patients who must stay in bed from painful pressure sores.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space

notes.text: Space and health, Telemedicine: Doctors on Earth keep track of astronauts' health from far away. Ideas from space medicine helped shape telemedicine, where doctors check on patients remotely. In the 1970s NASA tested it on the Tohono O'odham (then called Papago) reservation in Arizona, linking faraway clinics to doctors through television links.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space

notes.text: Space and health, Careers: Flight surgeons are doctors who care for astronauts. Space biologists, nutritionists, and psychologists help keep crews healthy on long missions.
notes.source_title: NASA: Muscle and exercise studies to maintain crew health in space
